title: Beyond the Prompt: Engineering Mindset for Vibe-Coding UX Designers

slides.title: Beyond the Prompt: Engineering Mindset for Vibe-Coding UX Designers
slides.lead: Moving from "it works on my screen" to resilient, scalable, and maintainable interfaces.
slides.note: Our working example: a list of saved projects.

slides.title: What a static frame leaves open
slides.lead: A Figma frame shows six saved projects. What should someone see before those projects arrive?

items.title: State
items.body: The frame captures one moment. Code needs rules for waiting, missing data, and transitions.

items.title: Speed
items.body: AI can draw six convincing rows in seconds. The data contract and tests still need decisions.

items.title: Intent
items.body: Design asks what the user expects. Engineering specifies the behavior each input should trigger.

slides.title: The demo works. What did it prove?
slides.lead: Cursor, v0, and Claude can turn a design idea into a working interface in one session.

items.title: What you can learn
items.body: With six sample projects, you can watch someone find a title, open a row, and return to the list.

items.title: What to test next
items.body: Try a slow connection and a second account. Check who can read each project and how many files a change touches.

slides.note: A happy-path demo can hide a permissions bug or a component that is hard to change.

slides.title: Give the component a contract
slides.lead: Start with the flow and visual hierarchy. Then describe the data and events that drive the screen.

items.title: A screen prompt
items.body: “Build a saved-projects page with a title, a list of projects, and an Open button.”

items.title: A component prompt
items.body: “ProjectList takes projects with an id and title, a request status, and an onOpen(id) callback. Show what happens when a request fails.”

slides.title: Design the four unhappy paths
slides.lead: Ask the AI to render each of these alongside the populated list before building the next feature.

items.title: Loading
items.body: Show skeleton rows during the first request so the layout stays steady.

items.title: Empty
items.body: After a successful request with zero results, offer “Create a project.”

items.title: Error
items.body: If the network request fails, explain what happened and offer “Try again.”

items.title: Partial
items.body: Keep available projects visible. Use a fallback for each missing thumbnail.

slides.title: Split the work by responsibility
slides.lead: An 800-line file mixing API requests, business rules, and Tailwind classes makes a small change risky.

items.title: Fetch
items.body: A data function requests projects and translates the API response into the agreed shape.

items.title: Manage state
items.body: A hook tracks the request, applies visibility rules to authorized data, and handles retry.

items.title: Present
items.body: A small, pure ProjectList renders its props and reports clicks. Reuse it with sample data in a preview.

slides.title: Give the next edit a clear boundary
slides.lead: A vague request and a whole-repo dump leave room for invented APIs and accidental rewrites.

items.title: Set the rules
items.body: Use project rules or a system prompt to name the stack, token library, and test command.

items.title: Name the files
items.body: Point to ProjectList.tsx and the existing request hook. Include their relevant contracts.

items.title: Give one task
items.body: “Add retry to the error state. Reuse the hook. Show the diff and the check you ran.”

slides.note: If an interface is missing, ask the agent to identify the gap before it edits.

slides.title: Make a save point before AI edits
slides.lead: Before a broad change, inspect git status and commit the working baseline. Start the experiment on a branch.

items.title: Build one behavior
items.body: Add retry, then test a failed request followed by a successful one.

items.title: Read the diff
items.body: Use git diff to spot unrelated edits. Stage only the changes that belong to this behavior.

items.title: Commit the result
items.body: Use git commit for each working micro-feature. If the experiment fails, return to the saved baseline.

slides.title: Read the diff and repeat the audit
slides.lead: You can review generated code even when you supplied none of the implementation.

items.title: Look for red flags
items.body: Check for hardcoded API keys, looping useEffect calls, lost keyboard focus, and new dependencies.

items.title: Get a fresh review
items.body: Give a fresh AI session the diff. Ask a staff engineer to identify risks by file and suggest a test for each.

items.title: Save the checklist
items.body: Put recurring accessibility, security, and component checks in SKILL.md or a custom command. Run it on each diff.

slides.title: Agree on what engineering inherits
slides.lead: Decide together whether the prototype is disposable or intended as production scaffolding.

items.title: Proof of concept
items.body: Record what users tried and what you learned. Label mock data and simulated permissions so engineering can rebuild deliberately.

items.title: Production scaffolding
items.body: Agree on tokens and shared components early. Remove dead code and hand over the data contract, decision notes, tests, and known gaps.

slides.title: Engineering fluency strengthens your design portfolio
slides.lead: Even if vibe coding isn’t for you, you can show a hiring team how you think through a design.

items.title: • Show a tradeoff
items.body: Walk through two ways to build a feature. Explain what each would cost users and why you chose one.

items.title: • Show a failure state
items.body: Include the screen someone sees when a save fails. Show how they can retry without losing their work.

items.title: • Show collaboration
items.body: Share a before-and-after from handoff. Point to the engineer’s feedback and the design decision it changed.

slides.title: Choose one habit for the next build
slides.lead: AI gets a working interface into your hands. Engineering habits help the next person change it safely.
slides.note: Commit one tested change. Design all four UI states. Or save one review skill.
